title: Pooh Counts Honey: Numbers 0 to 20 in the Hundred Acre Wood
topic: Counting, comparing, adding within 20, and estimating through Winnie-the-Pooh
lens: Winnie-the-Pooh by A. A. Milne (1926) and The House at Pooh Corner (1928)
description: Pooh loves honey and friends. In the Hundred Acre Wood, every pot, acorn, and paw print is something to count. Learners build number sense from 0 to 20: counting carefully, comparing more and fewer, adding and taking away, and estimating before they count. Inspired by books in the public domain in the United States. All illustrations are original.
author: Well of Wisdom contributors

lessons.title: Count every pot, once
lessons.summary: Count with one to one matching and say the last number is how many.

content.title: Pooh's row of pots
content.body:
Pooh has honey pots on a shelf. To know how many, Christopher Robin touches each pot once and says one number at a time: 1, 2, 3. The last number he says is the total. That is **counting** with care.

- Touch one thing, say one number
- Do not skip, do not count one thing twice
- The last number tells **how many**

Rabbit keeps his carrots the same way, in a neat row for counting.

content.prompt: Pooh counts pots: 1, 2, 3, 4. How many pots are there?
content.explanation: The last number counted is the total, so 4 pots.
content.hint: What was the last number he said?

content.prompt: Piglet lines up 7 acorns in a row. Tigger adds 3 more to the row. How many acorns are there now? Count on from 7.
content.hint: Start at 7 and count three more.

lessons.title: More, fewer, and the same
lessons.summary: Compare two groups and say which has more.

content.title: Who has more honey?
content.body:
Pooh has 5 pots. Piglet has 3. Put them in two rows and match them one to one. Two pots stick out on Pooh's side with nothing to match. Pooh has **more**, Piglet has **fewer**, and if they had the same number it would be **equal**.

- Line up, match, see what sticks out
- More means extra with no partner
- Equal means every pot has a partner and none sticks out

Eeyore's thistles can be compared the same way.

content.prompt: Row A has 9 leaves. Row B has 6 leaves. Which row has more?
content.explanation: 9 is more than 6, so row A has more.

content.prompt: Pooh and Piglet each collect 8 sticks. What can you say about the two groups?
content.explanation: Both have 8, so the groups are equal.

content.prompt: Kanga has 12 thistles. Roo has 9 thistles. How many more does Kanga have than Roo?
content.hint: Match Roo's 9 against Kanga's 12. How many stick out?

lessons.title: A little more: adding within 10
lessons.summary: Join groups and count the total.

content.title: One more pot for Pooh
content.body:
Pooh and Piglet put their honey together. 4 pots and 2 pots make 6 pots. That is **adding**, joining two groups into one.

- $4 + 2 = 6$ means four joined with two is six
- The plus sign means join. The equals sign means is the same as.
- A number line is a path. Start at 4, hop 2, land on 6.

Owl would call the total the sum. That just means how many in all.

content.prompt: 3 honey pots and 4 more pots are put on one shelf. How many in all?
content.hint: Join the two groups and count.

content.prompt: On a number line at 5, you hop 3 forward. Where do you land?
content.explanation: 5 plus 3 equals 8. Hopping forward on a number line is adding.

lessons.title: Taking away
lessons.summary: Eat or give away and see how many are left.

content.title: Pooh eats two
content.body:
Pooh has 8 pots. He eats 2. Now 6 remain. That is **subtracting**, taking away from a group.

- $8 - 2 = 6$ means eight take away two leaves six
- The minus sign means take away
- Count back to check. 8, 7, 6, yes.

If Tigger bounces off with 3, take away 3 more and count back again.

content.prompt: 9 acorns, 4 are given to Piglet. How many are left?
Which matches taking away on a number line?

choices.text: Start at 7, hop 2 back, land on 5
Start at 7, hop 2 forward, land on 9

content.explanation: Hopping back on a number line is subtracting.
content.hint: Taking away moves which way on the line?

lessons.title: Estimate before you count
lessons.summary: Guess close before you count close.

content.title: Owl estimates
content.body:
Owl likes to **estimate**, to guess close on purpose before counting. If he sees a scattered pile of about two rows of ten, he says about twenty. Then he counts to check. A good estimate is not wild. It is close enough to be useful.

- Look, think of a handy group like 5 or 10, then say about how many
- Then count one to one to check
- If you guessed 12 and counted 14, that was a good estimate. If you guessed 50, try using tens next time

content.prompt: A scattered picture shows about two tens worth of berries. Which is the best estimate?
content.explanation: Two groups of ten is about twenty.
content.hint: How many tens did you see?

content.prompt: Look around your room. Estimate how many books are on one shelf, then count and say whether your estimate was close.
content.answer: I estimated about 8 books and counted 9, so my estimate was close.
content.explanation: Any answer with an estimate and a check count and a judgement about closeness is good.

lessons.title: Make your Wood counting board
lessons.summary: A board, a row, and a shelf to play counting on paper.

content.title: Pooh's counting board
content.description: On cardboard, make three rows. On row one glue or draw up to 10 honey pot shapes. On row two make an addition row: draw a group, then another, then how many in all with a plus and equals sign. On row three make a subtraction row the same way. Add a row of real things to count at home and estimate before you do. Bring the board to the table and tell someone what each row shows.
content.rubric:
- Row one has up to 10 shapes counted one to one with the total written
- One correct addition within 10 with groups drawn and a number sentence
- One correct subtraction within 10 with groups drawn and a number sentence
- One estimate and count of real things with a note on how close
